text: What are the point of raking leaves? Lawn health and wildlife reasons. Raking leaves is done to keep fallen leaves from smothering the lawn, so grass can still get light and air before winter. Leaves left in heavy piles can block sunlight, trap moisture and attract pests. Raking is not always needed, since a thin layer can often stay in place.. Autumn leaf fall has renewed debate over whether homeowners should rake, mulch or leave leaves on the lawn. Bob Vila and This Old House have published new guidance on the question this season.. Experts disagree on how much to clear. Bob Vila notes that many specialists advise leaving leaves where they fall, because the leaf layer shelters birds, butterflies, moths and some native bees. The same source says that sending every leaf to the landfill removes that habitat and wastes a usable resource. Iowa State University warns that a dense leaf cover can stop turfgrass from building up food reserves before winter, which can leave dead patches open to weeds. The University of Maryland says heavy leaf litter also cuts air circulation and can keep grass damp long enough to encourage fungal problems. Wet leaves pressed flat by rain or snow cause the most trouble, so clearing them before a wet or snowy spell is the main reason given. North Carolina Cooperative Extension suggests that a light layer covering about 20% of the lawn can usually stay. At about 50% coverage, mowing the leaves into small pieces is often enough. The University of Minnesota advises collecting excess leaves once only about half of the lawn surface is visible, and says shredded leaves return phosphorus, potassium and some nitrogen to the soil as they decay.
